title: Milestone: The Physical World
objective: After this level you can connect landforms, water, climate and biomes into one picture of how Earth works.
summary: Earth works as connected systems: rock, water, air and life (plus ice). A breeze crossing a mountain shows them all at work, from rain to rain shadow to the biome on each side.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Time to see the physical world in one picture.
cards.body: You mapped the planet in Chapter 1 and toured its biomes in this one. Now zoom out. Rock, water, air and life aren't separate stories. They're parts of one machine.

cards.headline: Four spheres, one planet
cards.body: Scientists split Earth into connected systems. The geosphere is rock, from the crust down to the core. The hydrosphere is water, and Level 1 showed it covers about 71% of the surface. The atmosphere is the envelope of gas around us. The biosphere is all life. Many add a fifth, the cryosphere, for ice. And all of them constantly interact.

cards.headline: One breeze, every sphere
cards.body: Watch them team up. Moist air (atmosphere) climbs a mountain range (geosphere) and drops rain and snow on the way up (hydrosphere). The far side, starved of water, sits in a dry rain shadow. Which biome grows on each slope (biosphere) depends on how much heat and rain it gets. One breeze, and every sphere has a part to play.

cards.headline: Milestone: physical world connected
learned: How climate, land, water and life work together to decide which biome grows where.
Why climbing a tall mountain passes through the same climates as a trip toward the poles.
How plants survive their hardest season, from grass regrowing after fire to waxy needles in winter.
Why corals depend on the algae living inside them, and what makes a reef turn white.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits a biome?

options.label: A single pond and its fish
options.rationale: Far too small: biomes are huge regions.

options.label: Any country's national parks
options.rationale: Biomes ignore borders; climate and life define them.

options.label: A large region with its own plants and climate
A layer of rock deep underground
options.rationale: That's the geosphere, not a biome.

questions.explanation: A biome is a large area defined by its vegetation, soil, climate and wildlife.

questions.prompt: Which is the largest desert on Earth?

options.label: The Sahara
options.rationale: It's the largest hot desert, not the largest overall.

options.label: The Gobi
options.rationale: Much smaller than the record holder.

options.label: Death Valley
options.rationale: It's a rain shadow desert, far smaller.

questions.explanation: Deserts are defined by dryness, and icy, bone-dry Antarctica is the largest of all.

questions.prompt: Everest (Level 7) rises about 8,849 m. Why is its summit so much colder than the sea level below?

options.label: Air cools about 6.5 °C per 1,000 m climbed
It's farther from Earth's hot core
options.rationale: Height cools the air; the core isn't the reason.

options.label: It's closer to the North Pole
options.rationale: Its height, not its latitude, is the reason here.

options.label: The Sun never shines on the summit
options.rationale: The Sun shines there; the thin cold air is the reason.

questions.explanation: Air cools on average about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m. Nearly 9 km up, that adds up to a brutally cold summit.

questions.prompt: A mountain range leaves a desert in its rain shadow. Which two spheres are interacting most directly?

options.label: The biosphere and the cryosphere
options.rationale: Life and ice are not the main players here.

options.label: The hydrosphere and the cryosphere
options.rationale: The mountain itself is rock: the geosphere.

options.label: The biosphere and the hydrosphere
options.rationale: The key actors are the mountain and the moving air.

questions.explanation: Rock (the mountain, geosphere) forces air (atmosphere) upward, and the air drops its water before reaching the far side.

questions.prompt: A bleached coral is still alive. Why is it in danger?

options.label: Its skeleton has turned to sand
options.rationale: The skeleton is fine; the food supply isn't.

options.label: It has lost its main food source
White corals attract more predators
options.rationale: The danger is starvation, not predators.

options.label: It can no longer grip the seafloor
options.rationale: It stays fixed in place; it just starves.

questions.explanation: The expelled algae were the coral's main food. If the heat eases it can recover; if the stress lasts, it dies.

questions.prompt: Humboldt found Chimborazo's plant zones matched a trip toward the poles. Which idea from Level 41 explains that?

options.label: Mountains have their own special soil
options.rationale: Soil matters less than the heat and rain dials.

options.label: Plants spread downhill from the poles
options.rationale: It's the climate that repeats, not the plants migrating.

options.label: Latitude lines bend around mountains
options.rationale: Latitude lines don't bend; the climate changes with height.

questions.explanation: Height cools the air like latitude does, so similar climates, and similar biomes, appear on the mountain as on the way to the poles.

questions.prompt: Coral bleaching (Level 48) is a clear case of which two spheres interacting?

options.label: The geosphere and the atmosphere
options.rationale: No rock or air is doing the damage here.

options.label: The cryosphere and the geosphere
options.rationale: Ice and rock play no part in bleaching.

options.label: The atmosphere and the cryosphere
options.rationale: Bleaching happens in warm water, to living corals.

questions.explanation: Too-warm water (hydrosphere) makes living corals (biosphere) expel their algae and bleach.
